newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Moslems on trial for crimes against Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Moslems on trial for crimes against Serbs.

text.p: Scores of Bosnian Serbs were killed, tortured and raped at a prison camp in central Bosnia, a U.N. warcrimes tribunal heard on Monday when three Moslems and a Croat went on trial accused of atrocities.
Moslems Hazim Delic, Esad Landzo and Zejnil Delalic and Croat Zdravko Mucic are charged with war crimes against Serbs at the Celebici camp, near Konjic, during 1992.
"From the time the prison was first opened, the prisoners were subjected to horrible mistreatment," Swedish prosecutor Eric Ostberg told the opening session of the trial.
"Prisoners were murdered, tortured (and)..raped by soldiers who brought them to the prison, by guards at the prison, and by outside persons...permitted to come into the camp," he said.

Mucic, the 41-year-old former camp commander, and Delalic, 48 and a former Bosnian Moslem regional military leader, are accused of command responsibility for atrocities at the camp, including at least 14 murders and a grisly catalogue of torture, rape and sexual assault.
Deputy camp commander Delic, 32, is also charged with command responsibility and, along with 24-year-old camp guard Landzo, of actually taking part in torture, rapes and killings.
They are accused of beating elderly men to death with wooden planks, baseball bats, shovels and cable and of torturing with pliers, acid, electric shocks and hot metal pincers.
The trial is seen as a watershed for the Hague-based tribunal, set up in 1993 by the U.N. to punish war crimes committed during the bitter 3-1/2 year Bosnian conflict.
The first group trial, it is the first to focus on atrocities against Bosnian Serbs and the first in which command responsibility for war crimes is considered.
Ostberg told the packed court that the fact the accused were mainly Moslems, and the victims Serbs, should not become the focal point of the process.

"The religion or ethnicity of the perpetrators is of no consequence. The prosecution will vigorously object to any attempt...to turn this trial into anything but a trial of the individual responsibility of Delalic, Mucic, Delic and Landzo."
The tribunal has had to defend itself against accusations of anti-Serb bias, stating that its war crimes investigations are carried out irrespective of political or ethnic background.
Most of the 74 men it has so far charged are Serbs. Only seven suspects are actually in the tribunal's custody.
The four accused sat together in the dock, flanked by five U.N. guards. Mucic, a metalworker, and Landzo exchanged comments on several occasions, smiling and laughing.
Delalic, described by Ostberg as a successful building contractor and the crop-headed gum-chewing Delic, a locksmith, remained impassive throughout.
Delic and Landzo were arrested in Bosnia last May and handed over to the tribunal, the first time authorities in any former Yugoslav republic had exercised a tribunal arrest warrant.
Mucic was detained in Vienna and Delalic in Munich a year ago. All four claim to be innocent.
The trial's opening exchanges highlighted the difficulties the war has created for the court, with lawyers and presiding judge Adolphus Karibi-Whyte of Nigeria arguing over witnesses.
The defence wanted access to all prosecution witnesses, but prosecutors said this could jeopardise their safety.
"Without exception the witnesses have explicitly directed us not to give out their home addresses," U.S. prosecutor Teresa McHenry said. "Even asking the question frightened them."
The Celebici trial is the tribunal's third.
Judges are expected to announce their verdict in late April in the six-month trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic, accused of killing and torturing Moslems in northwest Bosnia in 1992.
Last November Croat Drazen Erdemovic was handed a 10-year jail sentence after pleading guilty to taking part in a Serb massacre of over 1,200 unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica in 1995.
He is appealing against the sentence.
